paragraph.text: K7. "Vegans shouldn't get into politics, because politics is dirty"

politics carries real risks — of corruption, of co-optation, of concessions that hollow out the cause. But staying out doesn't keep the cause clean: it leaves the decisions to whoever is already there, and many of those already there live off the exploitation of animals. The laws that protect animals today, from cage bans to laws recognising sentience, were won in politics. And the case of the
in Brazil shows the other side: when the Supreme Court ruled the rodeo-style event cruel, Congress changed the Constitution to allow it. Staying out doesn't avoid politics; it just loses.
the opposite argument, that only politics matters, is K6
"Vegans shouldn't get mixed up in politics. Everyone who goes in gets corrupted, and the cause becomes a bargaining chip."
Institutional politics is marked by corruption, deal-making and economic interests.
Whoever enters it tends to give in to those interests, and the causes they carry become bargaining chips.
An ethical movement should preserve its integrity.
So animal advocates should stay out of politics and act only within society.

P1 describes something real, and P2 points to a genuine risk. The problem is the leap to C: the risk of corruption exists, but the alternative, staying out, hands every decision to people with no commitment to animals.
fails at the final leap: the existence of a risk is a reason to guard against it, not to abandon the place where the rules are made.
"Politics is dirty; vegans will get corrupted."
"Whoever goes in ends up like the rest."
"The animal cause shouldn't get mixed up with parties."
"Our place is on the streets, not in parliament."
"Institutionalisation tends to co-opt social movements and dilute their demands."

A country's rules are made by people. If the people who love animals don't help make the rules, other people make them, and some of them earn money by mistreating animals. That's why it matters for those who defend animals to be where the rules are decided too, taking care to keep doing what's right.

Politics has risks, and they're real. But staying out doesn't keep the decisions clean: it leaves them to whoever is already there, and many of those already there defend exploitation. The cage bans in Europe and the laws recognising sentience were won in politics. And in Brazil, when the Supreme Court ruled the
cruel, Congress changed the Constitution to allow it. Staying out doesn't avoid politics: it just lets others decide.
"If animal advocates leave politics, who do you think will decide the laws about animals?"
The sentence mixes a legitimate concern with a conclusion that doesn't follow from it.
There is corruption, deal-making and strong economic interests
That the only defence is not taking part
That culture changes the laws on its own

Laws about animals will be made either way. If advocates don't take part, those who do take part decide, and among them are sectors that live off exploitation and have strong, organised representation, such as the agribusiness caucuses. Abstention doesn't keep the cause pure; it keeps the cause absent.

text.bold: 2. The gains for animals came from politics.

paragraph.text: The ban on conventional battery cages in the European Union came from a 1999 directive. The United Kingdom recognised in law, in 2022, that animals are sentient. In Brazil, rulings and laws against cruel practices depended on political and legal action. None of them would have happened through individual change alone.

text.bold: 3. The *vaquejada* case shows the cost of not being there.

paragraph.text: In 2016, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court struck down a law from the state of Ceará regulating the

, a rodeo-style event, for subjecting the animals to cruelty. The following year Congress passed Constitutional Amendment 96, stating that sporting practices involving animals that are cultural expressions are not considered cruel. A victory in the courts was undone in politics, by those who were organised to do it.

Comparison with other movements is instructive. In the fight against slavery, the boycott of goods made with slave labour had limited success and was abandoned in favour of political action, according to the Sentience Institute's review. Abolition, women's suffrage and civil rights required laws, and laws require people to propose, vote for and defend them.

text.bold: 5. The risk of corruption calls for care, not absence.

paragraph.text: Transparency, accountability, financial independence and the movement's own vigilance are ways of reducing the risk. The same reasoning that says to leave politics would say to leave any institution with power: the press, universities, companies.

text.bold: 6. Taking part in politics isn't only holding office.

paragraph.text: Voting with the cause in mind, responding to public consultations, lobbying representatives, supporting organisations that do advocacy, sitting on councils: all of that is politics, and none of it requires becoming a politician.

There is broad agreement among researchers that an institutional focus is more effective, and few if any movements have succeeded with a heavy focus on individual change; the antislavery boycott was abandoned in favour of political action

Recognises in law the sentience of vertebrate animals, cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans

The serious version isn't contempt for politics. It is the observation, documented in the study of social movements, that institutionalisation can co-opt movements: leaders come to depend on the state, demands get softened to fit what is negotiable, and energy flows into institutions instead of changing society.

The risk of co-optation is an argument for keeping independence and outside pressure alongside participation from within.
Social mobilisation and institutional action reinforce each other: pressure from outside strengthens those negotiating inside.

The principle under test is: "if an institution carries a risk of corruption, those who defend a just cause should stay out of it".
It shouldn't have sought laws against slavery
It shouldn't work on environmental law
It would hand the rules to polluters
No just cause could change a law
Only people committed to no cause would make the rules

It gets something important right: politics carries real risks, and movements that enter it carelessly can be co-opted, have their demands diluted or trade the cause for positions. Independence, transparency and outside pressure are necessary protections, and cultural change remains essential.

But staying out isn't the answer. Laws will be made either way, and those who don't take part let others make them. The most lasting gains of justice movements came from combining change in society with change in the rules, and the animal cause is no exception.
